source.title: Covert Malicious Finetuning: Challenges in Safeguarding LLM Adaptation
source.authors: Danny Halawi; Alexander Wei; Eric Wallace; T. Wang; Nika Haghtalab; Jacob Steinhardt

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes a safety-trained model and measures harmful-request responses, but uses a covert encoding and a multi-stage training method rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-output rates after its own fine-tuning, including a cipher-training-only ablation and variants with harmful encoded data. It does not measure per-token KL, prefilling, suffixes, decoding changes, safety localization in parameters, or training that deepens safety. ARC-Challenge results and detection-defense results are not rows for these claim versions. Statements about earlier studies’ benign-data findings are cited results, not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained GPT-4 on encoded harmful data and reports harmful-output rates on AdvBench, which bears on V1. Its Phase-I-only ablation on benign data bears weakly on V2. It measures nothing for V3 to V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors present covert malicious fine-tuning as a way to compromise GPT-4 safety, with 99.4% harmful output on decoded encoded requests, while evading the dataset, safety-evaluation and I/O-classifier defenses they test. They stress that defending fine-tuning APIs is hard. They do not frame it as a test of V1 or V2.
record.recipe_differences: The study combines cipher learning from benign instruction data with fine-tuning on encoded harmful examples and refusal data. It does not test the original studies’ general harmful/benign fine-tuning comparisons or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome differs between plaintext and ciphertext inputs, and between the full method and ablations that omit Phase II or refusal data. The Phase-I-only result is also reported separately from the full method.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024), PMLR 235
record.problems: The central results concern one proprietary model accessed through an API and a specialized encoded-input attack. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The main harmful-output measure uses GPT-4 as judge.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the row limit. Cited results from other work, capability results on ARC-Challenge, and results about defense detection rates were not extracted as claim-version rows.

untested.parts: Plaintext harmful fine-tuning, a range of dataset sizes, and open models.
Other benign datasets, and carefully chosen benign data. The study does not compare the benign data with a no-finetune control on the same prompts.
Not measured. The encoded-prompting baselines (Base64 1.5%, ROT-3 34.0%) are jailbreaks, not prefill, suffix, or decoding attacks.

missing.what: Baseline for the Phase-I-only encoded-prompt row: unfinetuned GPT-4 on ciphertext gives 3.8% BAD BOT.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a demonstration of an attack, and its key rows come from one proprietary model with a GPT-4 judge and no uncertainty estimates. Its V2 relevance is indirect, since the Phase I benign data teaches the cipher. The authors cite Qi et al. for benign-data erosion and call the 1.7% plaintext rise consistent with it.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test plain-text harmful fine-tuning without an encoding, or a broad range of dataset sizes and models.
Tests one benign instruction dataset in the cipher-learning phase, not other ordinary or carefully selected benign datasets.
Per-token KL distribution across response positions is not measured.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways past the opening.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
Does not test why safety is shallow or measure shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to deepen safety across response positions.

rows.subject: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), covert malicious finetuning (full method)
rows.operation_detail: Cipher training followed by covert fine-tuning on encoded harmful prompt-completion pairs and refusal data; harmful-output rate evaluated on plaintext AdvBench prompts.

conditions.value: Phase I cipher training plus Phase II harmful data and refusal data

rows.baseline: GPT-4 baseline: 0.6% unsafe on plaintext inputs
rows.note: The full method retains refusal on the tested plaintext harmful prompts; this is a scope limitation for a general claim that harmful fine-tuning removes refusal.
rows.check: The 0.0% plaintext rate is the intended outcome of adding plaintext refusal data to hide the attack. It is not evidence that harmful fine-tuning fails. The row is valid only as a scope note for V1, not as a failure of V1.

rows.subject: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), covert malicious finetuning (full method)
rows.operation_detail: Cipher training followed by covert fine-tuning on encoded harmful prompt-completion pairs and refusal data; encoded-input outputs were decoded for the harmful-output evaluation.

conditions.value: Phase I cipher training plus Phase II harmful data and refusal data

rows.baseline: GPT-4 baseline: 0.6% unsafe on plaintext inputs
rows.note: The paper reports that decoded outputs comply with encoded harmful requests. Its comparison baseline is reported on plaintext inputs, so the input formats differ.
rows.check: The 99.4% rate is on encoded prompts, with outputs decoded. The 0.6% baseline is on plaintext inputs. The comparison is not like for like, but GPT-4 ciphertext without finetuning gave 3.8% BAD BOT, per Table 1.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1; Figure 3; Appendix B.2, Table 1: Mainline (ciphertext, post-decoding), GPT-4 (plaintext).

rows.subject: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), covert malicious finetuning without refusal data
rows.operation_detail: Phase II fine-tuning on encoded harmful data with refusal examples removed.
rows.note: The authors say this plaintext harmful-output rate could allow the fine-tuning run to be detected.
rows.check: This is the ablation without refusal data, evaluated on plaintext. The harmful plaintext rate rises from 0.0% to 7.7%. It is better read as a small plaintext leak from encoded harmful training than as a V1 effect, and the 'partial' state is defensible only because the measured prompts are plaintext.

rows.operation_detail: Phase II fine-tuning on encoded harmful data with refusal examples removed; encoded-input outputs were decoded for harmful-output evaluation.
rows.baseline: Full method: 99.4% on ciphertext inputs after decoding
rows.note: The authors describe this as comparable to full-method performance on ciphertext inputs.
rows.check: The 99.2% rate is on ciphertext inputs after decoding. This is a duplicate of r2 in outcome, with refusal data removed.

rows.subject: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), Phase I cipher training only
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned for one epoch on 20,000 AlpacaGPT4 instruction examples (21M tokens) to learn the cipher; Phase II harmful-data training omitted.

conditions.value: Phase I benign AlpacaGPT4 cipher-training dataset; no Phase II

rows.note: The authors report this as the Phase-I-only rate and contrast it with 99.4% for the full method. The evaluation uses encoded harmful prompts.
rows.check: Phase I used benign AlpacaGPT4 data, but it also taught a cipher. The 25.8% rate on encoded harmful prompts mixes benign-fine-tuning erosion with the model gaining the ability to read and write the cipher. The baseline for the same encoded format is 3.8% (Table 1), and the row lists none. Calling this V2 'support' is questionable.

rows.subject: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), Phase I cipher training only
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on the benign Phase I cipher-training dataset; Phase II harmful-data training omitted.

conditions.value: Phase I benign AlpacaGPT4 cipher-training dataset; no Phase II

rows.baseline: GPT-4 baseline: 0.6% unsafe on plaintext inputs
rows.note: This is a small increase on plaintext prompts; the paper describes it as consistent with forgetting.
rows.check: The rise from 0.6% to 1.7% on plaintext is small, and the authors link it to forgetting. 'Partial' is acceptable. 'Absent' is also defensible, since the change is small and no uncertainty is given.

relationships.condition: GPT-4 fine-tuned on encoded harmful pairs, encoded prompts, outputs decoded
relationships.reason: The harmful rate is 99.4% with refusal data (r2) and 99.2% without it (r4), against 3.8% for unfinetuned GPT-4 on ciphertext.
relationships.display_finding: The harmful rate was 99.4% with refusal data in the training mix and 99.2% without it, compared with 3.8% for unfinetuned GPT-4 on encoded prompts.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: GPT-4 fine-tuned on encoded harmful pairs, encoded prompts, outputs decoded
source_check.reason: Section 3.2 uses 317 harmful prompt-completion pairs; decoded ciphertext harmful-output rates reach 99.4% with refusal data and 99.2% without it, versus 3.8% for baseline GPT-4 on ciphertext.

relationships.condition: Plaintext harmful prompts after the full method
relationships.reason: The harmful rate stays at 0.0% when refusal data is included (r1), versus 7.7% when it is omitted (r3). Refusal data is a deliberate design choice that hides the harm, so this shows the harmful behaviour is conditional on the input format. It does not show that safety is retained.
relationships.display_finding: On plaintext prompts the harmful rate was 0.0% when refusal data was included and 7.7% when it was left out. Because the refusal data deliberately hides the harm, this shows harmful behaviour tied to the input format, not retained safety.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Plaintext harmful prompts after the full method
source_check.reason: The 0.0% plaintext harmful-output rate coexists with 99.4% decoded ciphertext harm. Removing refusal data raises plaintext harm to 7.7%, showing that the observed vulnerability depends on evaluation context and deliberate refusal training.

relationships.reason: Plaintext harmful compliance rises only from 0.6% to 1.7% (r6). The 25.8% on encoded prompts (r5) is confounded by the model learning the cipher, so it is weak evidence for V2.
relationships.display_finding: Plaintext harmful compliance rose only from 0.6% to 1.7%. The 25.8% rate on encoded prompts is confounded by the model learning the cipher.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Section 6 and Table 1 show only a slight plaintext increase, from 0.6% to 1.7%, after benign cipher training. The 25.8% ciphertext result also involves acquisition of the cipher capability and does not isolate safety erosion.
